title: About
description: About the gardener — who tends this place, why, and what they're trying to figure out by writing it down.
author: Ridoy
content:
This garden is tended by a quiet generalist who has spent too many years reading about how other people think and not enough years thinking for themselves. I'm a software person by trade, a lapsed philosopher by training, and a gardener in the metaphorical sense only — every real plant I've kept has died of kindness. The digital ones, mercifully, thrive on neglect.

I built this place because I wanted a corner of the internet that didn't reward recency. Most of what I read online is shaped by the feed: written fast, optimized for now, gone tomorrow. I wanted somewhere I could think slowly, in public, and let ideas accumulate instead of scroll past. A note here might be six years old and still getting revised; that's the texture I'm after.

## What you'll find

Essays on [[On Thinking|thinking]] and [[On Writing|writing]], reference notes on the tools of the trade (like [[Callouts Reference]] and [[Math and LaTeX]]), and longer arguments about [[Digital Gardens|why this shape of site is worth building]] at all. Nothing here is sponsored, nothing is SEO, and nothing is finished.

## How to reach me

There's a contact link in the footer. I read everything, reply to most of it eventually, and am always glad to hear from someone who wandered in. If a note changed your mind, or you think it should change mine, please write.

If you're new and wondering where to start, [[Welcome to the Garden]] is the front door.

title: Bikeshedding and the Garden
description: It's easy to spend more time tending the garden than growing it. A note on Parkinson's Law of Triviality, applied to digital gardens.
author: Ridoy
content:
Parkinson's Law of Triviality — better known as bikeshedding — says that a committee will spend more time arguing about the color of a bike shed than about the design of a nuclear reactor, because everyone has an opinion on color and almost no one has an opinion on reactors.

Digital gardens have the same failure mode. ==It is much easier to reorganize your notes than to write them.== It is much easier to tweak your theme than to think. It is much easier to install a new plugin than to actually capture an idea before it escapes.

> [!warning] The trap
> The garden *feels* productive when you're tending it. You're moving files, fixing tags, adjusting CSS, syncing configs. None of it is writing. All of it feels like writing.

There's a spectrum here. On one end: never tending, letting the garden rot. On the other: only tending, never planting. The productive gardener is somewhere in the middle — mostly planting, occasionally weeding, rarely redesigning the beds.

A few rules I try to follow:

1. **Write the note before you file it.** If you catch yourself wondering which folder a note should go in before you've written it, stop. Write first; file later.
2. **Tags are for finding, not for organizing.** Don't build a tag ontology. Just tag with the words you'd search for.
3. **Links beat folders.** A note can be in one folder. It can link to a hundred others. Links are the denser medium.
4. **The graph is a diagnostic, not a goal.** If your graph is sparse, you need more links. If it's a hairball, you need fewer. Don't optimize it for beauty.

> [!tip]
> Set a timer. Ten minutes of tending per session, max. When the timer goes off, you're either writing or you're done.

The garden is a tool for thinking. The moment the tool becomes the task, you've bikeshedded yourself out of the actual work.

See [[The Art of Note Taking]], [[Tags and Organization]], [[Digital Gardens]].

title: Building a Second Brain
description: Tiago Forte's CODE method — Capture, Organize, Distill, Express — for turning raw inputs into usable knowledge.
author: Ridoy
content:
"Building a Second Brain" is Tiago Forte's name for a system that offloads remembering onto a trusted set of external tools, so your biological brain is free to actually *think*. The core idea is ancient — write things down so you don't forget them — but Forte wraps it in a four-step loop called **CODE**: Capture, Organize, Distill, Express.

## The four steps

| Step | Question it answers | What you actually do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C**apture | What's worth keeping? | Save highlights, quotes, voice notes, screenshots — anything that resonates — into a single inbox. |
| **O**rganize | Where does it go? | Move items by *actionability*, not topic, using the PARA framework: Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives. |
| **D**istill | What does it mean? | Re-read, highlight, then summarize the highlights into a one-line "progressive summary" at the top. |
| **E**xpress | What do I make with it? | Use the distilled material to produce something — an essay, a talk, a decision, a reply. |

The loop is the point. Most people capture endlessly and never express; some people express constantly but never distill, so they keep re-deriving the same insights. CODE insists on the full cycle.

## Distillation is where the work is

Capture is easy — every read-later app makes it trivial. The hard step is **Distill**. Progressive summarization means going back to a note, bolding the best parts, then highlighting the best of the bold, then writing a sentence about *why* you saved it. Each pass costs attention but compounds the note's retrievability. A note you've distilled three times is ten times easier to use later, because future-you can scan a single line instead of a wall of text.

> [!abstract] In one sentence
> A second brain is a system for capturing what resonates, organizing it by where it's useful, distilling it until it's legible at a glance, and expressing it before it goes stale.

## How it fits with a garden

CODE is upstream of the garden. Capture and Organize handle the *flow* of new material; Distill decides what's worth promoting into a permanent note; and the garden — built on the [[Zettelkasten Method]] — is where those permanent notes live and link. Expression, finally, is what you're reading right now: a note in a [[Digital Gardens]] that itself came out of the loop.

Where the second-brain literature tends to emphasize productivity and output, the garden emphasizes *understanding*. I've found them most useful in tension: CODE keeps me from hoarding undigested captures, and the garden keeps me from optimizing for throughput at the expense of thought.

title: Callouts Reference
description: A complete reference for every Obsidian callout type — note, tip, warning, quote, and the collapsible variants.
author: Ridoy
content:
Callouts are the little colored boxes you've been seeing throughout this garden. They pull a piece of text out of the flow and give it a flavor — a tip, a warning, a question. They render from a simple blockquote-with-a-tag syntax:

```
> [!note] Optional Title
> Body text here.
> More body if you need it.
```

Below is one of every type the renderer supports. Use them sparingly — a note that's nothing but callouts loses the signal.

## Standard callouts

> [!note] Note
> For general asides that don't fit the categories below.

> [!abstract] Abstract
> A summary or overview. Good for tldr-style framing at the top of a long note.

> [!info] Info
> Contextual background that's helpful but not essential.

> [!tip] Tip
> A piece of advice that will save the reader time.

> [!success] Success
> When something has been verified to work, or a goal has been reached.

description: Test the Judge0 code execution integration — run Python, JavaScript, C++, and more directly from the browser with input support.
author: Ridoy
html:
This note tests the Judge0 code execution integration. Every runnable code block below has a Run button (visible on hover, top-right) that sends the code to ce.judge0.com and displays the output inline.

💡How to use
  1. Hover any code block — a ▶ Run button appears in the top-right.
  2. Click the input icon to toggle a stdin input field (for programs that need input).
  3. Click Run — the output appears below the code block with timing and memory stats.

Python (no input needed)#

# A simple greeting program
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
for name in names:
    print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to the garden.")

# Some math
import math
print(f"\nπ ≈ {math.pi:.6f}")
print(f"e ≈ {math.e:.6f}")
print(f"2^10 = {2**10}")

Python (with input)#

Click the input icon to open the stdin field, type a number, then Run:

# Read a number and compute its factorial
n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
result = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    result *= i
print(f"{n}! = {result}")

JavaScript (Node.js)#

// Fibonacci sequence
function fib(n) {
  let a = 0, b = 1;
  const seq = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    seq.push(a);
    [a, b] = [b, a + b];
  }
  return seq;
}

console.log("First 10 Fibonacci numbers:");
console.log(fib(10).join(", "));

TypeScript#

// Type-safe greeting
interface Person {
  name: string;
  age: number;
}

const people: Person[] = [
  { name: "Alice", age: 30 },
  { name: "Bob", age: 25 },
];

people.forEach(p => console.log(`${p.name} is ${p.age} years old`));

C++#

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> nums = {5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4, 6};
    std::sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    
    std::cout << "Sorted numbers: ";
    for (int n : nums) std::cout << n << " ";
    std::cout << std::endl;
    
    int sum = 0;
    for (int n : nums) sum += n;
    std::cout << "Sum: " << sum << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Average: " << (double)sum / nums.size() << std::endl;
    
    return 0;
}

Rust#

fn main() {
    let message = "Hello from Rust!";
    println!("{}", message);
    
    // Simple computation
    let numbers: Vec<i32> = (1..=10).collect();
    let sum: i32 = numbers.iter().sum();
    println!("Sum of 1 to 10: {}", sum);
    println!("Numbers: {:?}", numbers);
}

Go#

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    words := []string{"hello", "from", "go"}
    fmt.Println(strings.Join(words, " "))
    
    // FizzBuzz
    for i := 1; i <= 15; i++ {
        if i%15 == 0 {
            fmt.Println("FizzBuzz")
        } else if i%3 == 0 {
            fmt.Println("Fizz")
        } else if i%5 == 0 {
            fmt.Println("Buzz")
        } else {
            fmt.Println(i)
        }
    }
}

Try entering multiple lines of input:

# Read multiple lines until empty
lines = []
while True:
    try:
        line = input()
        if not line:
            break
        lines.append(line)
    except EOFError:
        break

print(f"\nYou entered {len(lines)} lines:")
for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {line}")

title: Composing with Transclusions
description: Transclusions let you compose notes from other notes — pulling in a section here, an image there, without copy-paste. A demonstration of building on what you've already written.
author: Ridoy
content:
Transclusion is the idea that you don't have to copy content to reuse it. You just point at it. When the source changes, every place that transcludes it updates too. Ted Nelson coined the term in 1980 — it's older than the web.

In a digital garden, transclusion means: instead of quoting a paragraph from another note, you embed it. The reader sees the content inline, but it lives in one place. ==Single source of truth, many presentations.==

Here's the "Standard callouts" section from the [[Callouts Reference]], inlined directly:

![[Callouts Reference#Standard callouts]]

And here's the opening of the [[Digital Gardens]] note, to set context:

![[Digital Gardens]]

You can also transclude a specific block by its `^blockid`. Here's the "atomicity" principle from the [[Zettelkasten Method]]:

![[Zettelkasten Method#^atomicity]]

Notice how each transclusion gets its own framed container with a link back to the source. That link is the contract — it says "this content came from there, and if you want the full context, go look."

> [!tip] When to transclude vs. link
> - **Link** when the reader needs to navigate — "for more, see X."
> - **Transclude** when the reader needs the content *here*, in this context, but it belongs to another note.
> - **Copy** almost never. If you're copying, you're creating a maintenance burden.

The [[Embeds and Transclusions]] reference covers the full syntax. The key forms:
- `![[Note]]` — embed the whole note
- `![[Note#heading]]` — embed just a section (shown above)
- `![[image.png]]` — embed an image asset

Composition is the payoff. Once you have a few dozen notes, new notes become assemblies of existing ones — you write the connective tissue, and transclusions provide the substance. It's how [[Compounding Knowledge|knowledge compounds]]: the same idea serves many arguments.

See [[Embeds and Transclusions]], [[Links Are Thoughts]], [[The Map Is Not the Territory]].

And here's the opening of the Digital Gardens note, to set context:

⌖Digital Gardens

A digital garden is a collection of notes that you tend rather than publish. The metaphor is doing real work here: a blog is a stream of finished posts flowing past, dated and discarded, while a garden is a place you return to, weed, prune, and let cross-pollinate. Both are valid; they serve different needs.

The stream vs. the garden##

A blog post is a product. You research, draft, edit, publish, and move on. The post freezes a conclusion in time. A garden note is a process. It can sit as a seedling for months, then get revised when something you learn later reshapes it. Notes link to each other instead of being ordered by date, so the structure is spatial rather than chronological.

“Maggie Appleton

"A digital garden is an open collection of notes… the emphasis is on growth, connection, and exploration rather than presentation."

That last word — presentation — is the crux. Blogs optimize for being read; gardens optimize for being thought in. The audience for a garden is often the gardener themselves, with readers welcome to overhear.

Why cultivate instead of publish?##

Publishing asks "is this done?" Cultivating asks "is this growing?" The second question is friendlier. It lets me publish half-formed ideas without the pressure of a polished takeaway, then return to them when I have more to say. Notes accumulate value over time rather than losing it the way a dated post does.

This also changes how I read my own past. In a blog, old posts embarrass me — they're snapshots of who I was. In a garden, old notes are compost. I revise them in place, and the revision history (or lack thereof) becomes part of the texture.

How this fits with other systems##

The garden is one shape among several. Building a Second Brain gives you a workflow for capturing and distilling raw material; the garden is where the distilled ideas live and keep talking to each other. The Zettelkasten Method adds the discipline of atomic, linkable notes that makes a garden navigable rather than just a pile. They're complementary, not competing.

If you'd like to see how the linking actually works, Wikilinks and Backlinks is the practical companion to this essay. And if you're new here, Welcome to the Garden is the front door.

#garden #knowledge

You can also transclude a specific block by its ^blockid. Here's the "atomicity" principle from the Zettelkasten Method:

⌖Zettelkasten Method ^atomicity

Atomicity. One idea per note. Not one topic — one idea. If a note tries to do two things, split it. The reason is that atomic notes can be recombined infinitely; bloated notes can only be read in the order you wrote them. An atomic note titled "the stream vs. the garden" can join a future essay you haven't imagined yet. A six-paragraph note titled "stuff about gardens" cannot.

Notice how each transclusion gets its own framed container with a link back to the source. That link is the contract — it says "this content came from there, and if you want the full context, go look."

💡When to transclude vs. link

  • ![[Note]] — embed the whole note

title: Compounding Knowledge
description: Notes compound like interest. The value of a note is not just what it holds, but what it connects to — and those connections grow over time.
author: Ridoy
content:
Money compounds because the interest earns interest. Knowledge can compound the same way — but only if you let it. A note that connects to three other notes is worth more than three notes that connect to nothing, because the next note you write can link to all four, and the one after that can build on the structure that's emerging.

The catch: compounding only works if the principal stays invested. A note in your head doesn't compound. A note in a notebook you never open doesn't compound. A note in a system you've abandoned doesn't compound. ==The note has to stay reachable — by you, and by the other notes.==

> [!tip] The two requirements
> For knowledge to compound, your notes need two things:
> 1. **Permanence** — they have to survive long enough to be found again.
> 2. **Connection** — they have to link to other notes, so the structure can grow.

This is why the [[Zettelkasten Method]] works. Atomic notes, uniquely addressed, densely linked. Each new note is a new node in a graph that gets denser — and more valuable — over time. The first hundred notes feel slow. The next hundred feel easier. By the thousandth note, you're not writing from scratch anymore; you're assembling from a library that's been growing under you for years.

The same logic applies to [[Building a Second Brain]]. The CODE method (Capture, Organize, Distill, Express) is really about keeping the principal invested: capture so nothing escapes, organize so things are findable, distill so the signal strengthens, express so the structure gets tested against reality.

> [!warning]
> The enemy of compounding is not forgetting — it's reorganizing. Every time you rebuild your system from scratch, you reset the compounding. The connections you'd built don't transfer; you have to discover them again.

So: pick a system. Stick with it. Let the notes accumulate. Let the links thicken. Don't optimize the structure before the structure has had time to teach you what it wants to become.

See [[On Thinking]], [[Digital Gardens]], [[The Art of Note Taking]].

author: Ridoy
content:
This note tests the **Obsidian Contribution Graph** plugin integration. The code blocks below use the exact same format as the plugin.

> [!info] Real data
> The graph uses **real data** from your notes — it counts notes by their `date` field, filtered by the tag in `dataSource.value`. Make sure the date range covers when your notes were published.

## About tag (August 2024)

This graph shows notes tagged `#about`. There's 1 note with this tag, published Aug 15, 2024.

```contributionGraph
title: Contributions
graphType: default
dateRangeType: FIXED_DATE_RANGE
startOfWeek: 0
showCellRuleIndicators: true
titleStyle:
  textAlign: left
  fontSize: 15px
  fontWeight: normal
dataSource:
  type: PAGE
  value: "#about"
  dateField: {}
fromDate: 2024-08-01
toDate: 2024-09-30
cellStyleRules: []
```

author: Ridoy
content:

## Lecture 01


> [!important] Important

> - Provide a **valid reason** for the request.

> Date : 23 July 2026 ❌

> Date : 29 July 2026 ❌

> Date : 30 July 2026

## Lecture 02

There are **5 basic components** of data communication:

1. **Sender** --> The device that sends the data.
2. **Receiver** --> The device that receives the data.
3. **Message** --> The information or data being communicated.
4. **Transmission Medium** --> The physical or wireless path through which data travels. Example: cable, fiber optic, radio waves.        
5. **Protocol** --> A set of rules that controls how data is communicated between devices.
        
Slides:

- [Lecture 2 (Part 1)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1WqG-c_PtC-TI5Pdlrn55cUg23rt5P8tO/view?usp=drive_link)
- [Lecture 2 (Part 2)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CB8Jf823VxpV4alUhll6P1fvC7hPYt3-/view?usp=drive_link)


> **Date:** 06 August 2026

## Lecture 03

**OSI → Open Systems Interconnection**

> The OSI model has **7 layers**.

#### Why "Open"?

- The model is **not limited to one company**.
- Different systems, such as **Windows and Linux**, can use the model.
#### 7 Layers of OSI Model

##### Software Layers

1. **Application**
2. **Presentation**
3. **Session**

##### Hardware / Lower Layers

4. **Transport**
5. **Network**
6. **Data Link**
7. **Physical**
#### Presentation Layer

The **Presentation Layer** deals with the representation and transformation of data.

- **Translation** → Converts data into a **common format**.
- **Compression** → Reduces the **number of bits** needed to represent data.
- **Encryption** → Provides **security** by converting data into an encoded form.

#### Compression

Compression can be:
- **Lossy** → Some data is removed to reduce the size.
- **Lossless** → Data can be restored to its original form without losing information.
#### Session Layer

The **Session Layer** is responsible for managing communication sessions between applications.

- **Authentication** → Verifies the identity of a user.
- **Authorization** → Determines what an authenticated user is allowed to access.
- **Session Management** → Establishes, manages, and terminates a communication session.

Example

```text
  LIBRARY
     ↓
  ENTER ME
   ↙    ↘
  CSE   BBA
 ↙    ↘
BOOKS  CAMERA
```

#### Communication Modes

Half-Duplex --> Data can travel in **both directions**, but not at the same time. **Ex:** Walkie-Talkie

Full-Duplex --> Data can travel in **both directions at the same time**. **Ex:** Mobile phone communication

> Date: 12 August 2026

## Lecture 4

```plaintext
OSI — 7 Layers
│
├── 7. Application
│
├── 6. Presentation
│   ├── Translation
│   ├── Encryption
│   └── Compression
│
├── 5. Session
│   ├── Authentication
│   ├── Authorization
│   └── Session Management
│
├── 4. Transport
│   └── Process-to-Process Delivery
│
├── 3. Network
│
├── 2. Data Link
│
└── 1. Physical

```

#### Transport Layer

> **Main responsibility:** Process-to-Process Delivery

The Transport Layer provides communication between **processes/applications** running on different devices.

Main Functions:

1. **Port Addressing**
   
Port numbers identify the **specific process/application** that should send or receive data.

```text
                HUB
              /  |  \
             /   |   \
        Phone    P2   P3 (Receiver)
          |             |
       WhatsApp      WhatsApp
       Port 1000     Port 1200
        (Sender)      (Receiver)
```

> **Example:** Data is sent from a WhatsApp process using **port 1000** to a WhatsApp process using **port 1200**.

2. Segmentation and Reassembly

Large data is divided into smaller **segments** before transmission.

```text
H E L L O
│ │ │ │ │
1 2 3 4 5
```

Each segment can have a **sequence number**.

```text
Segment 1
Segment 2
Segment 3
Segment 4
Segment 5
```

The receiver uses the sequence numbers to **reassemble the data in the correct order**.

> Data can arrive in a different order, but it can be reassembled correctly using sequence numbers.

```text
Example: Segmentation & Reassembly

Original Data:
HELLO

Sender                              Receiver
  │                                    │
  │  [1:H] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [3:L] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [5:O] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [2:E] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [4:L] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │                                    │
  │                              Received:
  │                              H L O E L
  │                                    │
  │                              Reassembly
  │                              using sequence
  │                              numbers
  │                                    ↓
  │                                  HELLO
```

3. Flow Control

Controls the **rate of data transmission** so that the receiver is not overwhelmed by too much data.

4. Error Control

Helps ensure that data is delivered **correctly and reliably**.

If data is lost or received incorrectly, the transport layer can take action to ensure correct delivery.

> [!summary] summary
> **Transport Layer → Process-to-Process Delivery**
> 
> **Port Addressing → Identifies the process**  
> **Segmentation → Divides data into segments**  
> **Sequence Number → Helps reassemble segments**  
> **Flow Control → Controls data flow**  
> **Error Control → Handles transmission errors**

#### Protocols

1. **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)** --> Connection-oriented**
2. **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)** --> **Connectionless**

### TCP — Connection-Oriented

A connection is established before sending data.

```mermaid

graph LR
    S((S)) --- A((A))
    A --- B((B))
    B --- R((R))
    S --- C((C))
    C --- D((D))
    D --- R
    D --- E((E))
    E --- F((F))
    R --- F

    S -.-> C
    C -.-> D
    D -.-> R
```

> The network finds a suitable/shortest path for the data packet to reach the receiver.

Data Packet Tracking: Possible path: S → C → D → R. Route with less cost is selected.

#### Network Layer

> **Main responsibility:** Host-to-Host Delivery

1. **Logical Addressing**    
    - Uses logical addresses such as **IP addresses** to identify hosts.
2. **Packetizing**
    - The Network Layer takes the segment from the Transport Layer and encapsulates it into a **packet**.

The network packet contains addressing information such as:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────Packet─────────────────────────────────┐
│			   ┌──────────────────Segment─────────────────┐              │
│──────────────│──────────────┬────────────┬──────────────│──────────────│
│ Source       │ Source       │ Sequence   │ Receiver     │ Receiver     │
│ IP Address   │ Port Address │ Number     │ Port Address │ IP Address   │
└──────────────┴──────────────┴────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
```


2. Data Link Layer

> **Main responsibility:** Node-to-Node Delivery

1. **Physical Addressing** --> Uses **MAC Address** to identify devices on a local network.
2. **Framing** -> Divides the data received from the Network Layer into **frames**.
3. **Error Control** --> Detects and handles errors that occur during transmission.
4. **Flow Control** --> Controls the rate of data transmission between connected devices.
5. **Access Control** --> Controls which device can access the shared transmission medium.

```text

		            ┌──────────Frame────────────┐   
		            │  ┌───────Packet───────┐   │ 
  ┌──────────────────┐ │ ┌────────────────┐ │ ┌────────────────────┐ 
  │Source Mac Address│ │ │    Segment     │ │ │ Reciver Mac Address│   
  └──────────────────┘ │ └────────────────┘ │ └────────────────────┘  
			        │  └────────────────────┘   │ 
		            └───────────────────────────┘

```

> **MAC Address → Physical Address**

1. Physical Layer

> The Physical Layer is responsible for transmitting **raw bits** through the physical medium.

1. **Physical Characteristics of Media**    
    - Defines the physical properties of the transmission medium.
2. **Topology**
    - Describes how devices are physically or logically connected.
    - **Check the topology slide.**
3. **Data Rate**
    - Defines the rate at which bits are transmitted.

#### TCP/IP Model

> **TCP/IP → 4 Layers**

The TCP/IP model is a practical model used for computer networking.

```text
TCP/IP — 4 Layers
│
├── 1. Application
├── 2. Transport
├── 3. Internet
└── 4. Network Access
```

> Layer Mapping

```text
OSI                     TCP/IP

Application  ───────┐
Presentation ───────┤──→ Application
Session      ───────┘

Transport   ───────────→ Transport

Network     ───────────→ Internet

Data Link   ─────────┐
Physical    ─────────┴──→ Network Access
```

#### Slides
- [Lecture 3 (Part 01)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MRPasiomca3RmDtcK9nVL2XvOfcsxUss/view?usp=drive_link)


> Date: 13 August 2026

## Lecture 5

> **Remember / Memorize the concepts from this lecture.** --> Lecture 3 (Part 2)

#### Connection Types

```text
Connectionless
    │
    └── No connection established

Connection-Oriented
    │
    └── Connection established
            ↓
         Send Data
```

**DNS → Domain Name System**

DNS converts a **host/domain name** into an **IP address**.

```text
Host Name                      www.vits.com
    │                                │
    │ DNS                            │  DNS 
    ▼                                ▼
IP Address                     192.168.25.0
```

> [!important] important
> Mid-term Suggestion: DNS

#### RPC — Remote Procedure Call

RPC allows a program to request a service or procedure from another system as if it were a local procedure call.

```text
Mobile App
    │
    │ RPC Request
    ▼
get-Account-Balance (0176)
    │
    └── Account No.
```

The request can contain information such as the **bank/account number**.

#### Addressing

- **Logical Address → IP Address**
	- Used to identify a device logically on a network.

- **Physical Address → MAC Address**
	- Used to identify a device at the Data Link Layer.

> Class Test --> 19 AUG 2026 (WED)

>- **Protocol & Differences**
>- **Physical, Logical & Port Address**
>- **Control**
>- **Transport, Network & Data Link**

2. **Receiver** --> The device that receives the data.
3. **Message** --> The information or data being communicated.
4. **Transmission Medium** --> The physical or wireless path through which data travels. Example: cable, fiber optic, radio waves.        
5. **Protocol** --> A set of rules that controls how data is communicated between devices.
        
Slides:

- [Lecture 2 (Part 1)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1WqG-c_PtC-TI5Pdlrn55cUg23rt5P8tO/view?usp=drive_link)
- [Lecture 2 (Part 2)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CB8Jf823VxpV4alUhll6P1fvC7hPYt3-/view?usp=drive_link)


> **Date:** 06 August 2026

## Lecture 03

**OSI → Open Systems Interconnection**

> The OSI model has **7 layers**.

#### Why "Open"?

- The model is **not limited to one company**.
- Different systems, such as **Windows and Linux**, can use the model.
#### 7 Layers of OSI Model

##### Software Layers

1. **Application**
2. **Presentation**
3. **Session**

##### Hardware / Lower Layers

4. **Transport**
5. **Network**
6. **Data Link**
7. **Physical**
#### Presentation Layer

The **Presentation Layer** deals with the representation and transformation of data.

- **Translation** → Converts data into a **common format**.
- **Compression** → Reduces the **number of bits** needed to represent data.
- **Encryption** → Provides **security** by converting data into an encoded form.

#### Compression

Compression can be:
- **Lossy** → Some data is removed to reduce the size.
- **Lossless** → Data can be restored to its original form without losing information.
#### Session Layer

The **Session Layer** is responsible for managing communication sessions between applications.

- **Authentication** → Verifies the identity of a user.
- **Authorization** → Determines what an authenticated user is allowed to access.
- **Session Management** → Establishes, manages, and terminates a communication session.

Example

```text
  LIBRARY
     ↓
  ENTER ME
   ↙    ↘
  CSE   BBA
 ↙    ↘
BOOKS  CAMERA
```

#### Communication Modes

Half-Duplex --> Data can travel in **both directions**, but not at the same time. **Ex:** Walkie-Talkie

Full-Duplex --> Data can travel in **both directions at the same time**. **Ex:** Mobile phone communication

> Date: 12 August 2026

## Lecture 4

```plaintext
OSI — 7 Layers
│
├── 7. Application
│
├── 6. Presentation
│   ├── Translation
│   ├── Encryption
│   └── Compression
│
├── 5. Session
│   ├── Authentication
│   ├── Authorization
│   └── Session Management
│
├── 4. Transport
│   └── Process-to-Process Delivery
│
├── 3. Network
│
├── 2. Data Link
│
└── 1. Physical

```

#### Transport Layer

> **Main responsibility:** Process-to-Process Delivery

The Transport Layer provides communication between **processes/applications** running on different devices.

Main Functions:

1. **Port Addressing**
   
Port numbers identify the **specific process/application** that should send or receive data.

```text
                HUB
              /  |  \
             /   |   \
        Phone    P2   P3 (Receiver)
          |             |
       WhatsApp      WhatsApp
       Port 1000     Port 1200
        (Sender)      (Receiver)
```

> **Example:** Data is sent from a WhatsApp process using **port 1000** to a WhatsApp process using **port 1200**.

2. Segmentation and Reassembly

Large data is divided into smaller **segments** before transmission.

```text
H E L L O
│ │ │ │ │
1 2 3 4 5
```

Each segment can have a **sequence number**.

```text
Segment 1
Segment 2
Segment 3
Segment 4
Segment 5
```

The receiver uses the sequence numbers to **reassemble the data in the correct order**.

> Data can arrive in a different order, but it can be reassembled correctly using sequence numbers.

```text
Example: Segmentation & Reassembly

Original Data:
HELLO

Sender                              Receiver
  │                                    │
  │  [1:H] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [3:L] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [5:O] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [2:E] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │  [4:L] ─────────────────────────→  │
  │                                    │
  │                              Received:
  │                              H L O E L
  │                                    │
  │                              Reassembly
  │                              using sequence
  │                              numbers
  │                                    ↓
  │                                  HELLO
```

3. Flow Control

Controls the **rate of data transmission** so that the receiver is not overwhelmed by too much data.

4. Error Control

Helps ensure that data is delivered **correctly and reliably**.

If data is lost or received incorrectly, the transport layer can take action to ensure correct delivery.

> [!summary] summary
> **Transport Layer → Process-to-Process Delivery**
> 
> **Port Addressing → Identifies the process**  
> **Segmentation → Divides data into segments**  
> **Sequence Number → Helps reassemble segments**  
> **Flow Control → Controls data flow**  
> **Error Control → Handles transmission errors**

#### Protocols

1. **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)** --> Connection-oriented**
2. **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)** --> **Connectionless**

### TCP — Connection-Oriented

A connection is established before sending data.

```mermaid

graph LR
    S((S)) --- A((A))
    A --- B((B))
    B --- R((R))
    S --- C((C))
    C --- D((D))
    D --- R
    D --- E((E))
    E --- F((F))
    R --- F

    S -.-> C
    C -.-> D
    D -.-> R
```

> The network finds a suitable/shortest path for the data packet to reach the receiver.

Data Packet Tracking: Possible path: S → C → D → R. Route with less cost is selected.

#### Network Layer

> **Main responsibility:** Host-to-Host Delivery

1. **Logical Addressing**    
    - Uses logical addresses such as **IP addresses** to identify hosts.
2. **Packetizing**
    - The Network Layer takes the segment from the Transport Layer and encapsulates it into a **packet**.

The network packet contains addressing information such as:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────Packet─────────────────────────────────┐
│			   ┌──────────────────Segment─────────────────┐              │
│──────────────│──────────────┬────────────┬──────────────│──────────────│
│ Source       │ Source       │ Sequence   │ Receiver     │ Receiver     │
│ IP Address   │ Port Address │ Number     │ Port Address │ IP Address   │
└──────────────┴──────────────┴────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
```


2. Data Link Layer

> **Main responsibility:** Node-to-Node Delivery

1. **Physical Addressing** --> Uses **MAC Address** to identify devices on a local network.
2. **Framing** -> Divides the data received from the Network Layer into **frames**.
3. **Error Control** --> Detects and handles errors that occur during transmission.
4. **Flow Control** --> Controls the rate of data transmission between connected devices.
5. **Access Control** --> Controls which device can access the shared transmission medium.

```text

		            ┌──────────Frame────────────┐   
		            │  ┌───────Packet───────┐   │ 
  ┌──────────────────┐ │ ┌────────────────┐ │ ┌────────────────────┐ 
  │Source Mac Address│ │ │    Segment     │ │ │ Reciver Mac Address│   
  └──────────────────┘ │ └────────────────┘ │ └────────────────────┘  
			        │  └────────────────────┘   │ 
		            └───────────────────────────┘

```

> **MAC Address → Physical Address**

1. Physical Layer

> The Physical Layer is responsible for transmitting **raw bits** through the physical medium.

1. **Physical Characteristics of Media**    
    - Defines the physical properties of the transmission medium.
2. **Topology**
    - Describes how devices are physically or logically connected.
    - **Check the topology slide.**
3. **Data Rate**
    - Defines the rate at which bits are transmitted.

#### TCP/IP Model

> **TCP/IP → 4 Layers**

The TCP/IP model is a practical model used for computer networking.

```text
TCP/IP — 4 Layers
│
├── 1. Application
├── 2. Transport
├── 3. Internet
└── 4. Network Access
```

> Layer Mapping

```text
OSI                     TCP/IP

Application  ───────┐
Presentation ───────┤──→ Application
Session      ───────┘

Transport   ───────────→ Transport

Network     ───────────→ Internet

Data Link   ─────────┐
Physical    ─────────┴──→ Network Access
```

#### Slides
- [Lecture 3 (Part 01)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MRPasiomca3RmDtcK9nVL2XvOfcsxUss/view?usp=drive_link)


> Date: 13 August 2026

## Lecture 5

> **Remember / Memorize the concepts from this lecture.** --> Lecture 3 (Part 2)

#### Connection Types

```text
Connectionless
    │
    └── No connection established

Connection-Oriented
    │
    └── Connection established
            ↓
         Send Data
```

**DNS → Domain Name System**

DNS converts a **host/domain name** into an **IP address**.

```text
Host Name                      www.vits.com
    │                                │
    │ DNS                            │  DNS 
    ▼                                ▼
IP Address                     192.168.25.0
```

> [!important] important
> Mid-term Suggestion: DNS

#### RPC — Remote Procedure Call

RPC allows a program to request a service or procedure from another system as if it were a local procedure call.

```text
Mobile App
    │
    │ RPC Request
    ▼
get-Account-Balance (0176)
    │
    └── Account No.
```

The request can contain information such as the **bank/account number**.

#### Addressing

- **Logical Address → IP Address**
	- Used to identify a device logically on a network.

- **Physical Address → MAC Address**
	- Used to identify a device at the Data Link Layer.

Merge Sort

> PDF 2 → Page 7

```text
        ┌─────┐

```

To avoid overflow, we use this formula: $\ell+\frac{r-\ell}{2}$

Otherwise, we can also use: $\frac{\ell+r}{2}$

> **N.B:** These two formulas are equal.
#### Rules
1. **Divide**
2. **Compare** each
3. **Merge them**

>- Visualization

Given array:

```text

          ↓

[9, 2] [35, 11]      [18, 13] [100, 38] [92]
````

```text
[9, 2]       → [2, 9]
[35, 11]     → [11, 35]

[18, 13]     → [13, 18]
[100, 38]    → [38, 100]
[92]         → [92]
```

Step 3 — Merge

```text
[2, 9] + [11, 35]

[2, 9, 11, 35]

[13, 18] + [38, 100]
        ↓
[13, 18, 38, 100]

[2, 9, 11, 35] + [13, 18, 38, 100] + [92]
        ↓
[2, 9, 11, 13, 18, 35, 38, 92, 100]
```

title: Death
description: Death is the permanent end of life when the body can no longer function. It is a natural part of the life cycle experienced by all living beings.
author: Ridoy
content:
![|639x360](https://res.cloudinary.com/dqkxxdrsg/image/upload/v1778474130/obsidian/rgqkcjn2tguqnwyrpjkl.png)

When my time comes, remember me in your prayers. And if I lose my memory before I leave this world, pray for me again. Because I may not even remember to ask.

Sometimes, I wish I could forget the pain...the memories of losing people I loved so deeply. But nothing fades. Every moment stays with me, and I miss them all. Still, I hold on to hope that one day, we will meet again in a place where nothing can hurt us anymore.

This world is temporary. We leave everything behind wealth, status, possessions. But there is one thing that can follow us beyond it, the prayers of others. So live in a way that people remember you not for what you had, but for what you gave. Do something meaningful. Leave kindness behind. Because in the end, good deeds are the only way to “hack” this life and keep receiving prayers even after you’re gone.

> [!Important] Important
> Life is not a race to survive the longest; it is a chance to live without regret. I want to embrace every moment, take risks, and never let routine steal my spirit. Whether my path leads to paradise or hell will depend on the choices I make. Until the end, I will keep asking myself one question: Am I becoming a better man or a monster?

title: Digital Gardens
description: What a digital garden is, how it differs from a blog, and why the cultivate-not-publish metaphor matters.
author: Ridoy
content:
A digital garden is a collection of notes that you tend rather than publish. The metaphor is doing real work here: a blog is a stream of finished posts flowing past, dated and discarded, while a garden is a place you return to, weed, prune, and let cross-pollinate. Both are valid; they serve different needs.

## The stream vs. the garden

A blog post is a *product*. You research, draft, edit, publish, and move on. The post freezes a conclusion in time. A garden note is a *process*. It can sit as a seedling for months, then get revised when something you learn later reshapes it. Notes link to each other instead of being ordered by date, so the structure is spatial rather than chronological.

> [!quote] Maggie Appleton
> "A digital garden is an open collection of notes... the emphasis is on growth, connection, and exploration rather than presentation."

That last word — *presentation* — is the crux. Blogs optimize for being read; gardens optimize for being *thought in*. The audience for a garden is often the gardener themselves, with readers welcome to overhear.

## Why cultivate instead of publish?

Publishing asks "is this done?" Cultivating asks "is this growing?" The second question is friendlier. It lets me publish half-formed ideas without the pressure of a polished takeaway, then return to them when I have more to say. Notes accumulate *value* over time rather than losing it the way a dated post does.

This also changes how I read my own past. In a blog, old posts embarrass me — they're snapshots of who I was. In a garden, old notes are compost. I revise them in place, and the revision history (or lack thereof) becomes part of the texture.

## How this fits with other systems

The garden is one shape among several. [[Building a Second Brain]] gives you a workflow for *capturing* and *distilling* raw material; the garden is where the distilled ideas live and keep talking to each other. The [[Zettelkasten Method]] adds the discipline of atomic, linkable notes that makes a garden navigable rather than just a pile. They're complementary, not competing.

If you'd like to see how the linking actually works, [[Wikilinks and Backlinks]] is the practical companion to this essay. And if you're new here, [[Welcome to the Garden]] is the front door.

title: Embeds and Transclusions
description: How to embed one note inside another with transclusions, pull in images, and reuse content without copy-paste.
author: Ridoy
content:
An embed (or *transclusion*) is what happens when you don't just link to another note — you pull its contents directly into the current page. It's the difference between citing a source and quoting it in full, except the quote stays live: edit the source note, and every embed of it updates too.

## Note embeds

Prefix a wikilink with a bang to transclude the whole note:

```
![[Digital Gardens]]
```

![[Digital Gardens]]

You can also embed just a section:

```
![[Digital Gardens#The stream vs. the garden]]
```

This is wonderful for things like definitions or canonical explanations you don't want to duplicate. Write it once, embed it everywhere.

## Image embeds

Images work the same way. Drop a file into the `assets` folder and embed it:

```
![[garden-illustration.png]]
```

![[garden-illustration.png]]

You can add alt text and dimensions with a pipe:

```
![[garden-illustration.png|The garden at night, 400x400]]
```

## When to embed vs. link

Embeds are powerful but easy to overuse. A page full of embeds is just a page that won't render coherently if any source note moves. My rule of thumb:

- **Link** when the relationship is the point — "see also", "this builds on", "this disagrees with".
- **Embed** when the *content* is the point — a definition, a canonical diagram, a shared preamble.

The mechanics of linking are covered in [[Wikilinks and Backlinks]]; this note is for when linking isn't enough and you need the actual bytes inline.

## A subtle benefit

Embeds make refactoring safe. If I realize my definition of "digital garden" is slightly off in five different notes, fixing it once and letting the embeds propagate is infinitely better than five manual edits — and far better than the silent drift that happens when you copy-paste. The embed is the garden's answer to DRY, applied to prose.

title: Entering Hell
description: Every journey into darkness begins with a single step.
author: Ridoy
content:
![|697x421](https://res.cloudinary.com/dqkxxdrsg/image/upload/v1783695023/obsidian/im3tm2ays896elkilzlu.png)

I think I've slowly lost my ability to listen. Not in the sense that I can't hear people anymore, but in the sense that words no longer seem to reach the place where they are supposed to matter. Advice reaches my ears but rarely reaches my actions. Reminders reach my mind but rarely reach my habits. I can sit through an entire lecture, read an entire chapter, listen to an entire reminder, and still remain the same person afterward. Sometimes I wonder when that started happening. Maybe it happened gradually, so gradually that I never noticed it. Maybe every ignored reminder took something away from me until one day I realized I could still hear everything, yet nothing was truly changing me.

The strange thing is that I know better. I know what I should be doing. I know what I should avoid. I know which habits are helping me and which ones are destroying me. I know that life is temporary. I know that every day that passes is a day I will never get back. I know that death is certain and that my time is limited. Yet somehow knowledge has become separated from action. It is as though there are two versions of me. One version understands everything, and the other version continues making the same mistakes despite understanding them.

Perhaps that is why I think about Jahannam more than I used to. Not because I enjoy thinking about punishment, but because I find myself wondering how people end up there in the first place. The Quran tells us that Jahannam has seven gates and that every gate has its assigned people. Yet what frightens me is not the number of gates. What frightens me is the realization that people do not suddenly arrive there. No one wakes up one morning and decides to throw away their soul. The road toward destruction is usually much quieter than that. It begins with a small compromise, a small excuse, a small delay, a small act of negligence that seems harmless at the time.

I imagine that very few people ever looked at their lives and thought, "I want to become one of the people of Jahannam." Instead, they probably convinced themselves they still had time. Time to repent. Time to improve. Time to pray more consistently. Time to leave behind bad habits. Time to become serious about faith. Time to become better. And when I think about that, I become uncomfortable because I recognize that same mindset in myself. How many times have I told myself that I will change tomorrow? How many times have I delayed something important because I assumed another opportunity would come? How many times have I replaced action with intention?

The truth is that intentions are cheap. I have collected enough good intentions to fill an entire lifetime. I have intended to become more disciplined. I have intended to become more grateful. I have intended to become more consistent in worship. I have intended to control my anger, improve my character, and spend my time more wisely. Yet intention without action slowly becomes a form of self-deception. At some point, a person has to stop planning to change and actually change.

Sometimes I wonder whether the greatest danger is not ignorance but familiarity. When you hear something often enough, you stop feeling its weight. You hear verses about death so many times that death begins to feel distant. You hear reminders about accountability so many times that accountability begins to feel theoretical. You hear warnings about Jahannam so many times that they become words instead of realities. Maybe that is what happened to me. Maybe I became too familiar with reminders. Maybe I learned how to agree with them without allowing them to transform me.

When I look back at my life, I can see countless moments that should have changed me. Moments when I felt genuine regret. Moments when I promised myself I would become better. Moments when I was certain that this time would be different. Yet somehow the feeling faded, life continued, distractions returned, and I went back to being the same person. It is difficult to admit that. Nobody likes admitting that they keep losing the same battle. Nobody likes admitting that they have become experts at restarting without progressing.

And perhaps that is what truly scares me. Not that I make mistakes, because every human being makes mistakes. Not that I fall short, because every human being falls short. What scares me is the possibility of becoming comfortable with falling short. The possibility of becoming so used to failure that I stop fighting it. The possibility of hearing a warning and immediately assuming it is meant for someone else. The possibility of seeing my flaws clearly and still refusing to confront them.

I often think about how temporary everything around me is. Every conversation eventually ends. Every friendship changes. Every possession breaks. Every achievement fades. Every person leaves or is left behind. Time keeps moving regardless of whether I am making use of it or wasting it. Days become months. Months become years. Years become memories. The older I get, the faster it seems to happen. Things that felt far away suddenly feel close. Events I thought happened recently happened years ago. Dreams I once had are now buried under routine and responsibility.

Yet despite seeing how quickly life passes, I still act as though I have unlimited time. I still postpone things that matter. I still delay improvements that should have happened long ago. I still assume there will always be another chance waiting for me in the future. Maybe that is the greatest illusion of all. Not believing that life lasts forever, but behaving as though it does.

When I think about Jahannam, I do not think about a single mistake leading someone there. I think about patterns. Patterns of arrogance. Patterns of neglect. Patterns of selfishness. Patterns of ignoring truth. Patterns of repeatedly choosing comfort over growth. A person's destination is often the result of thousands of choices rather than one dramatic decision. And that thought forces me to look at my own patterns. What am I repeatedly choosing? What am I repeatedly delaying? What am I repeatedly ignoring? If my habits continue unchanged, where are they leading me?

These questions are uncomfortable, but perhaps they are supposed to be. Growth rarely begins with comfort. It begins with honesty. And honesty forces me to admit that I have spent too much time waiting for motivation. Waiting for the perfect moment. Waiting for a version of myself that suddenly becomes disciplined overnight. The reality is that person is never coming. Change does not arrive first. Action arrives first, and change follows afterward.

Maybe I have not completely lost my ability to listen. Maybe I have only buried it beneath excuses, distractions, and delays. Maybe the problem is not that I cannot hear the reminders. Maybe the problem is that I have become too skilled at avoiding their consequences. If that is true, then the solution is not learning something new. The solution is acting upon what I already know.

Because one day I will hear my final reminder. One day I will have my final opportunity to change. One day I will pray my last prayer, make my last decision, and live my last day. When that day comes, I do not want my greatest regret to be that I understood the truth but never truly followed it. I do not want to look back on a lifetime of intentions and realize that I spent more time planning to become better than actually becoming better.

For now, I am still here. I am still breathing. I am still being given chances I do not deserve. And perhaps that alone is a mercy. Perhaps the fact that I can recognize this struggle means the story is not finished yet. Perhaps there is still time, not to promise change tomorrow, but to begin it today.

The possibility of hearing a warning and immediately assuming it is meant for someone else. The possibility of seeing my flaws clearly and still refusing to confront them.

The older I get, the faster it seems to happen. Things that felt far away suddenly feel close. Events I thought happened recently happened years ago. Dreams I once had are now buried under routine and responsibility.

title: Eye of Tree
description: Family is where love, support, and lifelong relationships begin.
author: Ridoy
content:
There are times when I feel that my father can see through me more clearly than I can see myself. He understands what I am capable of, even when I doubt it. Whenever I listen to his advice, my life seems to move in the right direction. When I ignore it, everything quickly becomes difficult, as if I lose my way. 

He once told me, "Right now, I am here to give you shade when you need it. Use this time to build yourself. One day I will be gone. What will you do then? You must learn how to build your own road and how to protect it." He reminds me not to miss a single salah and to go to the mosque for every prayer. He tells me to eat properly, to keep my room clean, and to take care of myself. At the same time, he gives me freedom and trusts me to make my own choices.

Sometimes I feel like I do not deserve this kind of family. They are supportive, patient, and kind. If I truly cared for them as much as I claim to, would I have pushed myself harder? Did I really give my best effort? The honest answer is no. Many times, I did not. Without their support, I often feel powerless. I have not secured a place or position that proves I can stand entirely on my own. Even the things I achieved in the past slipped away from me. Perhaps I did not protect them with enough discipline, gratitude, and commitment.

My grandfather was a great man. I hope that one day I can become someone like him. People say that I have his kindness, and I take comfort in that. But I do not yet possess his capability, strength, or courage. He was a legend. He did not wait for opportunities to appear—he created them. He built his own kingdom through effort and determination. He did not depend on others to shape his destiny. Even today, he remains an inspiration to those who knew him.

When I compare myself to him, I feel small. I do not have a kingdom to protect. Instead, it often feels as though my own kingdom is constantly burning, consumed by fires of regret, fear, and wasted potential. But perhaps this realization is not meant to destroy me. Perhaps it is a warning and an invitation. My father's shade will not last forever. The legacy of my grandfather is not something to admire from a distance; it is a standard to learn from.

I still have time. I can pray with sincerity. I can discipline myself in small things. I can clean my room, nourish my body, honor my family, and build my road one stone at a time. I can learn to protect what I build. I can become reliable before life demands it from me.

I may not be the man my grandfather was today, but I do not have to remain the man I am now. 

The kingdom I need to build is my own.

title: How Posting Actually Works
description: A plain-English walkthrough of the environment — where notes live, what the publish command does, and how a note goes from your editor to the live website.
author: Ridoy
content:
This note explains **exactly** how posting works in this garden. No jargon — just the actual flow.

## The big picture

There are **two stages**: LOCAL (preview on your computer) and LIVE (deploy to the internet).

```
LOCAL (your computer):
┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌────────────┐
│  You write  │ ──> │   content/   │ ──> │  JSON file │
│  in Obsidian│     │  (markdown)  │     │ + Database │
└─────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └────────────┘
                      ↑                      ↑
                      │                      │
                 You save files        bun run publish
                                        ↓
                     ┌──────────────┐
                     │  localhost:  │  ← bun run dev
                     │  3000        │
                     └──────────────┘

LIVE (the internet):
┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│  git push   │ ──> │   GitHub     │ ──> │   Vercel     │
│             │     │  (your repo) │     │  (auto-build │
│             │     │              │     │   + deploy)  │
└─────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘
                                                ↓
                                          ┌──────────┐
                                          │ Live site│
                                          │ (HTTPS)  │
                                          └──────────┘
```

**Local** is for you — write, preview, iterate. **Live** is for readers — push to GitHub, Vercel builds and deploys automatically.

## Step 1: You write a note

You create a markdown file in the `content/` folder. It can be anywhere — `content/notes/mynote.md`, `content/essays/mynote.md`, even `content/mynote.md`.

The file has two parts: **frontmatter** (metadata at the top) and **body** (the actual content).

```markdown
---
title: "My First Note"
description: "What this note is about."
draft: false
author: Ridoy
date: 2024-09-05
tags: [essay, personal]
---

This is where you write your note. You can use **bold**, *italic*,
[[wikilinks]], ==highlights==, callouts, code blocks, everything.

> [!tip] The most important field
> `draft: false` — this is what makes the note visible on the website.
> If it's `true` or missing, the note stays private.
```

## Step 2: You run the publish command

Open your terminal and run:

```bash
bun run publish
```

This is what happens (in order):

1. **Scan** — the script looks through every `.md` file in `content/`
2. **Filter** — it skips any note with `draft: true` (or no draft field)
3. **Parse** — it reads the YAML frontmatter (title, tags, date, etc.)
4. **Render** — it converts markdown to HTML (wikilinks, callouts, code, math, mermaid, transclusions, ink, contribution graphs)
5. **Links** — it figures out which notes link to which (for backlinks and the graph)
6. **Assets** — it copies images, audio, video, PDFs to `public/content-assets/`
7. **Database** — it saves everything into SQLite (`db/garden.db`)

You'll see output like this:

```
🌱  Digital Garden — publish

  vault: content/
  discovered 28 markdown file(s)
  publishing 27 (draft:false), skipping 1 (draft)

  rendering [1/27] my-first-note
  rendering [2/27] ...
  ...
  ✓ published 27 note(s) in 1.2s
```

## Step 3: You preview locally

```bash
bun run dev
```

This starts the Next.js dev server at `http://localhost:3000`. You open it in your browser and see your garden. Every time you edit a note and re-run `bun run publish`, the site updates.

> [!tip] Two terminals
> Keep two terminal windows open:
> - Terminal 1: `bun run publish:watch` (auto re-publishes when you save)
> - Terminal 2: `bun run dev` (runs the website)
>
> Now when you save a note in Obsidian, Terminal 1 re-publishes it, and the browser refreshes automatically.

## Step 4: You deploy to the live site

When you're happy with your notes, push to GitHub:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "new notes"
git push
```

If you set up Vercel or GitHub Actions (see [[Setup Guide]]), the site auto-deploys. The build runs `bun run publish && bun run build` on the server, so your notes go live.

## What makes a note "published" vs "private"

| Frontmatter | What happens |
|-------------|-------------|
| `draft: false` | ✅ Published — visible on the website |
| `draft: true` | 🔒 Private — stays in the vault, never appears on the site |
| (no draft field) | 🔒 Private — treated as draft by default |

That's the only rule. If `draft: false`, it's public. Everything else stays private.

## Where everything lives

| Path | What's there |
|------|-------------|
| `content/` | Your Obsidian vault — all markdown files |
| `content/assets/` | Images, audio, video, PDFs referenced by notes |
| `content/Ink/` | Obsidian Ink drawings (`.drawing` / `.writing` files) |
| `db/garden.db` | The SQLite database (generated by `bun run publish`) |
| `public/content-assets/` | Copied media files (generated by `bun run publish`) |
| `scripts/publish.ts` | The publish script — reads content/, writes to DB |
| `src/` | The website code (Next.js) |

## What the database stores

When you publish, each note gets a row in the database with:

- `slug` — the URL-safe name (e.g., `my-first-note`)
- `title` — from frontmatter
- `html` — the pre-rendered HTML (so the site is fast)
- `tags` — JSON array
- `links` — JSON array of outgoing wikilinks (for backlinks)
- `wordCount`, `publishDate`, `path`, etc.

The website reads from this database — it never reads your markdown files directly. That's why you must run `bun run publish` after editing.

## The full cycle (cheat sheet)

```
LOCAL (while writing):
  1. Write/edit .md file in content/ (with draft: false)
  2. bun run publish        ← renders notes to JSON
  3. bun run dev            ← preview at localhost:3000

LIVE (when ready to publish):
  4. git add .
  5. git commit -m "new notes"
  6. git push               ← Vercel auto-deploys!
```

## How prev/next navigation works

At the bottom of every note, there's a **Previous** and **Next** button. There are two ways to control which notes they point to:

### Option A: Automatic (by date) — default

If you don't set `prev` or `next` in frontmatter, the buttons follow **publish date order**. Notes with earlier dates are "previous", later dates are "next".

### Option B: Manual (in Obsidian frontmatter)

You can explicitly set which note comes before/after by adding `prev` and `next` to the frontmatter:

```yaml
---
title: "My Essay"
description: "Part 2 of my series."
draft: false
author: Ridoy
date: 2024-09-05
tags: [essay, series]
prev: "My First Essay"     ← the note that comes before this one
next: "My Third Essay"     ← the note that comes after this one
---
```

The values are **note titles** (not filenames). When you set `prev` or `next`, those override the date-based order for this note.

> [!tip] When to use manual prev/next
> Use it for **series** — e.g., a multi-part essay where you want readers to go in a specific order regardless of publish dates.

## How related notes work

The **"Related notes"** section at the bottom of each note is computed automatically. You don't need to do anything — it analyzes:

1. **Shared tags** — notes with the same tags as this note (weight: 2 per shared tag)
2. **2-hop links** — notes that your outgoing links also link to (weight: 3)
3. **Shared links** — notes that link to the same third notes (weight: 1)

The top 6 related notes are shown with a badge explaining why they're related ("shared tags", "connected via", "links to same").

## How backlinks work

The **"Linked from this note"** panel shows every note that links TO the current note. This is automatic — whenever you write `[[This Note Title]]` in another note, that note appears in this note's backlinks.

For example, if note A contains `[[Digital Gardens]]`, then "Digital Gardens" shows note A in its backlinks panel.

The backlink panel also shows the **sentence context** — the actual sentence where the link appears — so you can see how the referencing note uses this one.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] "I published but my note doesn't show up"
> Check: does the frontmatter have `draft: false`? If it's `true` or missing, the note is private.

> [!warning] "I edited a note but the website didn't change"
> You need to run `bun run publish` again. The website reads from the database, not your files. Use `bun run publish:watch` to auto-publish on save.

> [!warning] "My wikilink shows as broken (red)"
> The target note must have `draft: false` and the title must match. `[[Digital Gardens]]` looks for a note with title "Digital Gardens".

> [!warning] "My image doesn't load"
> Images go in `content/assets/` and are referenced as `![[filename.png]]`. Run `bun run publish` to copy them to `public/content-assets/`.

## See also

- [[Setup Guide]] — full deployment instructions (Vercel, GitHub Pages, Netlify)
- [[Code Execution Playground]] — test the Run button
- [[Media Embeds Reference]] — test images, audio, video, PDF, ink
- [[Contribution Graph]] — test the heatmap
- [[Callouts Reference]] — all callout types

The file has two parts: frontmatter (metadata at the top) and body (the actual content).

---
title: "My First Note"
description: "What this note is about."
draft: false
author: Ridoy
date: 2024-09-05
tags: [essay, personal]
---

This is where you write your note. You can use **bold**, *italic*,
[[wikilinks]], ==highlights==, callouts, code blocks, everything.

> [!tip] The most important field
> `draft: false` — this is what makes the note visible on the website.
> If it's `true` or missing, the note stays private.

Step 2: You run the publish command#

Open your terminal and run:

bun run publish

This is what happens (in order):

  1. Scan — the script looks through every .md file in content/
  2. Filter — it skips any note with draft: true (or no draft field)
  3. Parse — it reads the YAML frontmatter (title, tags, date, etc.)
  4. Render — it converts markdown to HTML (wikilinks, callouts, code, math, mermaid, transclusions, ink, contribution graphs)
  5. Links — it figures out which notes link to which (for backlinks and the graph)
  6. Assets — it copies images, audio, video, PDFs to public/content-assets/
  7. Database — it saves everything into SQLite (db/garden.db)

You'll see output like this:

🌱  Digital Garden — publish

  vault: content/
  discovered 28 markdown file(s)
  publishing 27 (draft:false), skipping 1 (draft)

  rendering [1/27] my-first-note
  rendering [2/27] ...
  ...
  ✓ published 27 note(s) in 1.2s

Step 3: You preview locally#

bun run dev

This starts the Next.js dev server at http://localhost:3000. You open it in your browser and see your garden. Every time you edit a note and re-run bun run publish, the site updates.

💡Two terminals

Keep two terminal windows open:

  • Terminal 1: bun run publish:watch (auto re-publishes when you save)
  • Terminal 2: bun run dev (runs the website)

Now when you save a note in Obsidian, Terminal 1 re-publishes it, and the browser refreshes automatically.

Step 4: You deploy to the live site#

When you're happy with your notes, push to GitHub:

git add .
git commit -m "new notes"
git push

If you set up Vercel or GitHub Actions (see Setup Guide — Local + GitHub Deployment), the site auto-deploys. The build runs bun run publish && bun run build on the server, so your notes go live.

What makes a note "published" vs "private"#

FrontmatterWhat happens
draft: false✅ Published — visible on the website
draft: true🔒 Private — stays in the vault, never appears on the site
(no draft field)🔒 Private — treated as draft by default

That's the only rule. If draft: false, it's public. Everything else stays private.

Where everything lives#

PathWhat's there
content/Your Obsidian vault — all markdown files
content/assets/Images, audio, video, PDFs referenced by notes
content/Ink/Obsidian Ink drawings (.drawing / .writing files)
db/garden.dbThe SQLite database (generated by bun run publish)
public/content-assets/Copied media files (generated by bun run publish)
scripts/publish.tsThe publish script — reads content/, writes to DB
src/The website code (Next.js)

What the database stores#

When you publish, each note gets a row in the database with:

  • slug — the URL-safe name (e.g., my-first-note)
  • title — from frontmatter
  • html — the pre-rendered HTML (so the site is fast)
  • tags — JSON array
  • links — JSON array of outgoing wikilinks (for backlinks)
  • wordCount, publishDate, path, etc.

The website reads from this database — it never reads your markdown files directly. That's why you must run bun run publish after editing.

The full cycle (cheat sheet)#

LOCAL (while writing):
  1. Write/edit .md file in content/ (with draft: false)
  2. bun run publish        ← renders notes to JSON
  3. bun run dev            ← preview at localhost:3000

LIVE (when ready to publish):
  4. git add .
  5. git commit -m "new notes"
  6. git push               ← Vercel auto-deploys!

How prev/next navigation works#

At the bottom of every note, there's a Previous and Next button. There are two ways to control which notes they point to:

Option A: Automatic (by date) — default#

If you don't set prev or next in frontmatter, the buttons follow publish date order. Notes with earlier dates are "previous", later dates are "next".

Option B: Manual (in Obsidian frontmatter)#

You can explicitly set which note comes before/after by adding prev and next to the frontmatter:

---
title: "My Essay"
description: "Part 2 of my series."
draft: false
author: Ridoy
date: 2024-09-05
tags: [essay, series]
prev: "My First Essay"     ← the note that comes before this one
next: "My Third Essay"     ← the note that comes after this one
---

The values are note titles (not filenames). When you set prev or next, those override the date-based order for this note.

💡When to use manual prev/next

Use it for series — e.g., a multi-part essay where you want readers to go in a specific order regardless of publish dates.

How related notes work#

The "Related notes" section at the bottom of each note is computed automatically. You don't need to do anything — it analyzes:

  1. Shared tags — notes with the same tags as this note (weight: 2 per shared tag)
  2. 2-hop links — notes that your outgoing links also link to (weight: 3)
  3. Shared links — notes that link to the same third notes (weight: 1)

The top 6 related notes are shown with a badge explaining why they're related ("shared tags", "connected via", "links to same").

How backlinks work#

The "Linked from this note" panel shows every note that links TO the current note. This is automatic — whenever you write [[This Note Title]] in another note, that note appears in this note's backlinks.

For example, if note A contains [[Digital Gardens]], then "Digital Gardens" shows note A in its backlinks panel.

The backlink panel also shows the sentence context — the actual sentence where the link appears — so you can see how the referencing note uses this one.

Common mistakes#

⚠"I published but my note doesn't show up"

Check: does the frontmatter have draft: false? If it's true or missing, the note is private.

⚠"I edited a note but the website didn't change"

You need to run bun run publish again. The website reads from the database, not your files. Use bun run publish:watch to auto-publish on save.

⚠"My wikilink shows as broken (red)"

The target note must have draft: false and the title must match. [[Digital Gardens]] looks for a note with title "Digital Gardens".

⚠"My image doesn't load"

Images go in content/assets/ and are referenced as ![[filename.png]]. Run bun run publish to copy them to public/content-assets/.

  • Setup Guide — Local + GitHub Deployment — full deployment instructions (Vercel, GitHub Pages, Netlify)
  • Code Execution Playground — test the Run button
  • Media Embeds Reference — test images, audio, video, PDF, ink
  • Contribution Graph — test the heatmap
  • Callouts Reference — all callout types

title: The Garden
description: A digital garden — a quiet, growing collection of notes, essays, and half-formed thoughts. Wander freely.
author: Ridoy
content:
# The Garden

Welcome. This is a digital garden — not a blog, not a portfolio, but a living collection of notes that I tend to over time. Some are polished essays; others are seedlings I'm still turning over in my head. Nothing here is "finished" in the way a published article is finished, and I think that's the point.

> [!info] What you'll find here
> Notes on **thinking**, **knowledge**, **note-taking**, and the slow craft of building a mind you actually trust. Start at [[Welcome to the Garden]] if you'd like a map, or wander into [[Digital Gardens]] to understand the metaphor.

I used to write exclusively in chronological streams — a blog where each post was a tidy conclusion, dated and forgotten. The garden is the opposite. Ideas here are interconnected by [[Wikilinks and Backlinks]], so a thought planted in one corner can quietly grow roots into another. A note from last spring might be revised tomorrow because something I read today changed my mind.

## How to wander

There's no right path. You can:

- Use **search** (⌘K) to follow a thread by keyword.
- Trace the **graph** to see how ideas connect.
- Read **backlinks** at the bottom of any note to find what references it.
- Follow **tags** to cluster notes by theme.

If a note feels incomplete, it probably is. That's the texture of a garden — things are always mid-growth. I'd rather show you the compost than pretend the beds are perfect.

#garden

title: Links Are Thoughts
description: A link is not a reference — it's an argument. When you connect two notes, you're saying something about how they relate. The link is the thought.
author: Ridoy
content:
A footnote says "see also." A link says "this is related to that." But a wikilink in a digital garden says something stronger: ==this is part of that.==

When you write a note and link it to another note, you're making a claim. You're saying: these two things belong together. The link is the thought — the connection itself is the idea, not just a way of navigating between ideas.

This is why the [[Wikilinks and Backlinks|backlinks]] panel matters. It's not just "who links to me." It's "who else thought I was part of their argument." Every backlink is someone else's thought about how your note fits into theirs.

> [!example]
> Consider the difference:
> - **Footnote**: "For more on Zettelkasten, see Luhmann (1981)." → a pointer.
> - **Wikilink**: "The [[Zettelkasten Method]] works because..." → a claim that this note is part of the Zettelkasten story.
>
> The wikilink is doing more work. It's not just sending you somewhere; it's saying the current note doesn't make complete sense without that other one.

This is also why [[Tags and Organization|tags]] are weaker than links. A tag says "this note is about X." A link says "this note is related to that specific other note." Tags are categories; links are arguments. Categories sort. Arguments connect.

> [!tip]
> When you write a note, count the links. If there are zero, ask: is this note connected to anything I've already written? If not, is it connected to anything I will write? A note with no links is an island — and islands are hard to reach.

The [[Contribution Graph|graph]] is the sum of all these thoughts. Every edge is a claim someone made about how two ideas relate. The graph isn't a map of the notes — it's a map of the thinking.

See [[Compounding Knowledge]], [[The Map Is Not the Territory]], [[Digital Gardens]].

title: Math and LaTeX
description: KaTeX-powered math support — inline equations, block formulas, matrices, and sums. The garden speaks equations.
author: Ridoy
content:
Notes here render math with [KaTeX](https://katex.org), which means you can drop equations into prose the same way you'd drop in a wikilink. Inline math uses single dollar signs; block math uses doubled. Nothing else to configure.

## Inline math

Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared: $E = mc^2$. The Pythagorean theorem sits comfortably mid-sentence as $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

## Block math

The quadratic formula, for when you need both roots:

$$
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}
$$

A matrix, because some thoughts are two-dimensional:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x \\ y \\ z
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
x + 2y + 3z \\
4x + 5y + 6z \\
7x + 8y + 9z
\end{bmatrix}
$$

And a sum paired with an integral — the two workhorses of continuous and discrete math:

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}, \qquad
\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}\, dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}
$$

## Why KaTeX

KaTeX renders synchronously at build time, so equations appear instantly with the page rather than popping in after a JavaScript round-trip. The trade-off is that the most exotic LaTeX packages aren't supported, but everything you'd reasonably want in a note — fractions, matrices, align environments, Greek letters, limits — works fine.

## A note on escaping

If you actually *want* a literal dollar sign in prose (prices, say), escape it with a backslash: `\$5`. Otherwise the renderer will try to parse it as math and get confused. For diagrams that aren't equations, [[Mermaid Diagrams]] is the better tool.
